title: Punjab's shared devotional ground
hook: a song from a Marathi tailor turns up in Punjab, and a boy keeps his eye on a kite string

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan ended with the poet-sadhus, and their songs of watching, longing and letting go. Did you tell someone what you love about them? Day one thousand four hundred six.

A boy on a rooftop is flying a paper kite. His friends are around him, laughing, teasing, talking over each other, and he's laughing with them. But watch his hands. Watch his eyes. Whatever he's saying, part of him never leaves the string. That picture comes from a song. The song was made by Namdev, the tailor-saint of Maharashtra we met last year, singing to Vitthal. And the song is kept far to the north, in Punjab, in a book Sikhs honor as their living Guru. Today we cross into Punjab, where devotional songs from many places ended up living side by side.
screen: `A BOY AND A KITE.` → `A SONG FROM MAHARASHTRA.` → `KEPT IN PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: Punjab is a crossroads, and the songs show it. Start with the book. The Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs revere as their Guru, holds the hymns of the Sikh Gurus. It also holds songs by bhagats, devotees from outside that line: Namdev from Maharashtra, Kabir the weaver of Kashi, Ravidas, and Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of Punjab, among others. Sikhs sing them in the gurdwara alongside the Gurus' own hymns. Hindus honor Namdev, Kabir and Ravidas in their own traditions too. So here is ground that both share, and each stands on it in its own way. Then Namdev himself. Tradition says that late in life he traveled north and lived in Punjab, and a village there, Ghuman, remembers him with a shrine. A tailor from the Marathi country, honored in a Punjabi village. Songs travel with people, and sometimes people travel with songs. And now the kite. In that hymn, in paraphrase, Namdev gives a string of pictures. A boy flies his kite and talks with his friends, but his mind stays on the string. Young women carry water pots on their heads, laughing and chatting as they walk, but their attention stays on the pot. A cow grazes far out in the fields, but her mind is on her calf. A mother goes about her work, but her heart is on the child in the cradle. That's how, the song says, the mind can stay on God: not by stopping life, but in the middle of it. The kite is still flying. The talk goes on. Underneath, one thread holds.
screen: `PUNJAB, A CROSSROADS OF SONG` · `SAINTS FROM MANY PLACES IN ONE BOOK` · `NAMDEV REMEMBERED IN A PUNJAB VILLAGE` · `THE MIND ON THE STRING`

segments.voice: Hold the string for two minutes. Sit, and let the breath settle. Let sounds come and go around you, traffic, voices, a fan, the way the friends chatter around the boy on the roof. Don't push them away. Just let one light thread of attention stay on your breath, the way his fingers stay on the kite string. When you notice you've let go, pick the string back up. If you pray, the thread can be a name of God. The bell holds the time.
Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, a song by Namdev, kept in Punjab, about a mind that holds its string in the middle of everything. Today's word.
Your line: Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, in one busy moment, a meal, a meeting, a commute, keep one finger on the string: one breath, noticed. Day one thousand four hundred six.

howItsDone: Namdev's hymns are sung by Varkaris in Maharashtra and, from the Guru Granth Sahib, in gurdwaras; in Ghuman, Punjab, a shrine honors him.
